## Methods

Sample preparation
The layered catalysts were prepared via a solid-state method based on a previous literature51. A stoichiometric amount of specific raw reactants, including Li2CO3 (99.9%, Aladdin), Co3O4 (99.9%, Macklin), Fe2O3 (≥99%, Aladdin), NiO (99%, Aladdin), Pd(NO3)2 (0.216 M, Kojima Chemicals Co., Ltd.), Na2CO3 (≥99.5%, Macklin), K2CO3 (99.5%, Macklin), (MgCO3)4·Mg(OH)2·5H2O (98%, Macklin), MnO2 (99%, Aladdin), RuO2 (Ru 75.2% min, Alfa Aesar), Ce(NO3)3 (≥98%, Wako), Cr2O3 (99%, Aladdin), La2O3 (99.9%, Aladdin), TiO2 (P25, Macklin), MoO2 (99%, Aladdin), ZnO (99%, Dieckmann), Cu(OH)2 (≥96%, Macklin), CoCl2·6H2O (99.99%, Aladdin), CoSO4·7H2O (99%, Aladdin), and LiF (99%, Aladdin), were mixed well and then sintered for 12 h in ambient air with a heating ramping rate of 10 °C min−1. The thermal treatment temperature for catalyst preparation has been optimized, and 700–850 °C is suitable for LCO (Fig. S46), among which 800 °C is chosen as the sintering temperature in this research considering proper kinetics and high-purity phase.

α-Co(OH)2 was synthesized by CoCl2·6H2O (1 mmol, 99.99%, Aladdin) and NaCl (99.5%, Aladdin, 2.5×g), both of which were dissolved in ultrapure water (150 mL, 18.2 MΩ cm) with stirring (solution A). NH3·H2O (0.133 mL, 25–28%, Aladdin) was mixed with ultrapure water (50 mL) and dropped into solution A under stirring by a peristaltic pump (10 mL h−1). The precipitation was washed by ultrapure water and finally dried.

β-Co(OH)2 was prepared by dropping CoSO4·7H2O (0.1 M, 10 mL, 99%, Aladdin) into a stirring NaOH aqueous solution (0.2 M, 10 mL, 96%, Aladdin). After stirring for one hour, the precipitation was rinsed three times by centrifugation with ultrapure water and finally dried.

The XRD of synthesized α-Co(OH)2 and β-Co(OH)2 are presented in Fig. S47.

RuO2 (Alfa Aesar), IrO2 (Aladdin), Co3O4 (99.9%, Macklin), and NiFe2O4 (≥99.5%, Aladdin) were used without further treatment.

Characterizations
XRD measurements were conducted on an X-ray diffractometer (PANalytical X’Pert3 Powder, Cu Kα, λ=0.15406 nm). The corresponding Rietveld refinements were performed with the General Structure Analysis System (GSAS-II) program. The XAFS and sXAS were collected at the TLS 01C1 and TLS 20A1 beamlines of the National Synchrotron Radiation Research Center, Taiwan. The XANES and EXAFS data were processed and analyzed using the Demeter software package Athena52, and the energy at the maximum value of the first derivative of its XANES was defined as the E0 for energy correction. The EXAFS results of the Co K edge were fitted by Artemis52. Wavelet transform was used to analyze the EXAFS data by a self-developed program53. XPS results were obtained on a Thermo Fisher Nexsa spectrometer using an Al Kα source. For ex-situ XRD and XAS characterizations, catalyst powders were loaded onto carbon paper substrates prior to the OER measurements. The preparation of post-OER sample involved 10 CV cycles (5 mV s−1, 1.02–1.62 V vs. RHE, 1 M KOH, 22 °C or 50 °C) during which the current stabilized. Subsequently, a 30-min chronoamperometry hold at 1.62 V vs. RHE was applied during which no notable current decay was observed. The samples were then rinsed with deionized water and dried under vacuum at 25 °C for 12 h before characterization.

HAADF-STEM images were taken by JEOL-2100F equipped with an energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy detector. A field emission SEM (Zeiss SIGMA 500) mounted with an energy-dispersive X-ray detector was used for morphology and elemental analysis. Raman spectra were collected in a Raman spectrometer (Renishaw inVia Qontor) with the laser at 100 mW (0.05% intensity) and 532 nm. In-situ Raman spectroscopy was performed using a GSL (Gaoss Union) electrochemical cell coupled to the instrument. Measurements employed a 532 nm excitation source with a three-electrode configuration: carbon cloth (Toray Industries) working electrode, Pt wire counter electrode (Gaoss Union), and Ag/AgCl reference electrode (Gaoss Union, 1 M KCl solution) in 1 M KOH electrolyte. The system was stabilized at each potential for 15 min prior to spectral acquisition, which commenced precisely at the 10-min interval. An Iontof 5 spectrometer was used for the ToF-SIMS measurements. The analysis was done with a pulsed 30 keV Bi+ primary ion source and the depth profiling by sputtering with a 1–2 keV Cs+ beam. The pressure was 10−7 Pa. IonSpec software was used for data acquisition and post-processing analysis. Negative ion profiles were recorded due to their sensitivity to fragments originating from oxide matrixes. ICP-MS (NexION 350D Perkin-Elmer) with a mass resolution of 0.3–3.0 a.m.u. was conducted to measure element concentration. The mass variation was characterized by EQCM (10 M Gamry Instruments Inc.) with a working electrode of a gold quartz crystal (5 MHz). EPR spectra were recorded with a Bruker EMXplus X-band spectrometer (≈9.84 GHz) at 25 °C. The spectra were averaged over 5 scans with 1000 points per sweep. Each 2 mg sample was measured under identical settings. The g‑factor was calculated using g=hν/βH. Oxygen vacancy concentrations were quantified by comparing EPR peak areas.

Electrochemical assessment
The OER activity was evaluated in 1 M KOH (≥95%, Macklin) with a three-electrode set-up measured by an electrochemical workstation (Gamry 1010E). The electrolyte was freshly prepared before each experiment using ultrapure (18.2 MΩ·cm) water (150 mL) as the solvent. It was then stored sealed in a chemical-resistant glass reagent bottle and used on the same day. Glassy carbon (Gaoss Union, 3 mm, <50 °C) and carbon paper (Toray Industries, 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm, to avoid catalyst peeling off at the reaction temperature ≥50 °C) were utilized as working electrode, and graphite rod (Gaoss Union), and Ag/AgCl (Gaoss Union, 1 M KCl filling solution) served as counter and reference electrode, respectively. The catalyst ink was prepared by dispersing the mixture of 6 mg of active material with 2 mg of Vulcan XC-72 carbon into a solution made of 0.95 mL ethanol (AR, Uni-Chem) and 0.05 mL of 5 wt% Nafion under ultrasonic treatment for 30 min, and 1 mg cm−2 active material was covered on working electrode by drop casting. The measured potentials were calibrated to the RHE scale using the following equation: ERHE = EAg/AgCl + E0Ag/AgCl + 2.303·RT·pH/F, where E is the measured potential with respect to the Ag/AgCl reference electrode and E0 is the standard reference electrode potential and obtained by Eq. (1)54:

E0Ag=AgCl(T) = 0.23659 − 4.8564×10−4(T−273.15) − 3.4205×10−6(T−273.15)2 − 5.869×10−9(T−273.15)3 (1)

T is the operation temperature, R is the ideal gas constant (8.31 J K−1 mol−1), F is the Faraday constant (96485 C mol−1). The pH value of 1 M KOH electrolyte was measured as 13.8±0.1, 13.2±0.1, and 12.5±0.1 was obtained in 25, 50, and 80 °C, respectively. CV and LSV were conducted at a scan rate of 5 mV s−1 in the tests. The ECSA was measured within a non-Faradaic potential window of 1.15–1.20 V vs. RHE at scan rates of 1, 2, 4, 8, and 10 mV s-1, as shown in Fig. S9a, c, e, and g. For each scan rate, the current difference at a selected potential (1.175 V vs. RHE) was calculated as (Ia-Ic)/2, where Ia and Ic are the anodic and cathodic currents at the selected potential, respectively. The double-layer capacitance (Cdl) was obtained by plotting (Ia-Ic)/2 versus scan rate (mV s−1) and fitting the data to a linear regression (Fig. S9b, d, f, and h). The slope of this line yielded Cdl in units of capacitance (F). The ECSA was then calculated using ECSA = Cdl/(Cs·m), where m is the loading mass of the catalysts on the electrode and Cs is the reference capacitance per unit area (40 μF cm−2 55). Notably, the catalyst ink used for ECSA testing was prepared without the addition of XC-72 carbon. The test temperature was controlled by a thermostatic water bath (Sunne Inc., Shanghai, China). EIS was obtained using a Gamry 1010E electrochemical workstation over a frequency range from 1 MHz to 0.1 Hz at 1.65 V vs. RHE with an AC amplitude of 10 mV.

MEA preparation and single-cell tests
The MEAs were fabricated using a hand spray-coating method for both the anode and cathode catalyst layers. The anode catalyst ink was prepared by dispersing the catalyst powder in a mixed solvent of deionized water and isopropanol (mass ratio=1:4:5). Subsequently, 5 wt% Nafion solution was added, resulting in a Nafion content of 7 wt% in the final ink. The ink was ultrasonicated for 1 h to ensure homogeneous dispersion and then uniformly sprayed onto a nickel foam substrate (Kunshan Shengshijingxin New Material Co., Ltd, China, 1 cm2). The anode catalyst loading was controlled at 10.0±0.5 mg cm−2 (1 mg cm−2 for RuO2 and IrO2), determined by weight difference before and after coating. For the cathode, a 5 wt% Pt/C catalyst (Alfa Aesar) was used. The ink formulation consisted of catalyst, deionized water, and isopropanol in a weight ratio of 1:8:9. After adding 5 wt% Nafion solution (final Nafion content 10 wt%), the ink was ultrasonicated for 1 h and then sprayed onto a carbon paper substrate (TGP-H-120T, Toray). The Pt loading was 0.5 mg cm−2.

A commercial Sustainion® membrane (X37-50, Grade T, Dioxide Materials) was employed as the anion exchange membrane for all single-cell tests. Prior to use, the membrane was pre-treated by soaking in 1 M KOH for 12 h to ensure full ion exchange. The MEA was assembled with an active geometric area of 1.0 cm2 (as shown in Fig. 6a). The single cell hardware was composed of nickel-coated stainless-steel end plates to ensure chemical stability in alkaline media.

All electrochemical measurements were conducted in 1 M KOH electrolyte, supplied to both anode and cathode chambers. Polarization curves were recorded at 80 °C by a Gamry 5000E electrochemical workstation with 30 s hods at each current density ranging from 0.10 A cm−2 to 2.50 A cm−2, followed by a reverse scan. Voltage and current density data were recorded during the downward scan. The durability of the MEA was evaluated by operating the cell at a constant current density of 500 mA cm−2 at 60 °C with a programmable DC power supply (Tommense TM-K1560SPL).

High-frequency resistance (HFR) was measured via EIS using a Gamry 5000E electrochemical workstation over a frequency range from 1 MHz to 1 Hz at a cell potential of 1.8 V with an AC amplitude of 10 mV. The HFR was obtained from the intercept of the Nyquist plot with the real axis. Three independent measurements were performed, and the mean and standard deviation were subsequently calculated from the replicate data. The voltage data are presented without iR compensation unless specifically indicated.

Three-electrode AEMWE preparation
The anode and cathode used in three-electrode AEMWE are the same with the two-electrode AEMWE introduced above, and the only difference is the membrane. Versogen A40 membrane (thickness 40 μm) was used. Prior to use, the membrane was equilibrated under ambient laboratory conditions for 1 h before removing the protective films. This step allows the bicarbonate form of the membrane to convert to the hydroxide form, which is required to achieve optimal ionic conductivity. To ensure full conversion to the hydroxide form, the membrane was immersed in 0.5 M KOH aqueous solution at 22 °C for 1 h, after which the solution was replaced with freshly prepared 0.5 M KOH and the membrane was immersed for an additional 1 h. Following the two-step soaking process, the membrane was rinsed thoroughly with deionized water until the rinse water reached approximately neutral pH (~7). During handling, exposure of the membrane to ambient air was minimized to prevent CO2 uptake, which would convert the membrane back to the bicarbonate form. Three-electrodes system was established based on our homemade cell (Fig. S45a). The membrane was extended to an extra reference electrode chamber (Fig. S45b) and filled with 0.01 M KOH to ensure good ionic conduction with Ag/AgCl reference electrode. The testing procedure is the same with two-electrode single cell.

Anode applied potential breakdown analysis: the sources of potential loss at the anode was identified using a three-electrode AEMWE setup (Fig. S45a, b) to study the transport properties of LCNFPdO and LCO. The polarization curves of individual anode and cathode versus Ag/AgCl (1 M KCl solution) reference electrode and the calculated full cell voltage are shown in Fig. S45c, d.

The calculated full cell voltage is obtained from the individual electrode potentials according to Eq. (2):

Ecalculatedfullcell(j) = Eanodevs:Ag=AgCl(j) − Ecathodevs:Ag=AgCl(j) (2)

where Eanodevs:Ag=AgCl and Ecathodevs:Ag=AgCl are the potentials versus Ag/AgCl reference electrode obtained during tests.

The total anode potential breakdown model can be written as Eq. (2) 56:

Eanode(j) = Erev,OER + ΔEkinetic(j) + ΔEohmic(j) + ΔEmasstransport(j) (3)

where Eanode (vs. RHE) is the anode potential applied, Erev,OER is the reversible potential for OER, and ΔEkinetic, ΔEohmic, and ΔEmasstransport are the kinetic, ohmic, and mass transport potential losses, respectively. The Eanode is obtained using Eq. (3):

Eanode(j) = EAg=AgCl(j) + E0Ag=AgCl + 2.303× RT/F × pH (4)

And the Erev,OER = 1.1812 V (vs: RHE) is calculated using Eq. (5) 57:

E0rev,OER = 0.4011 − 1.6816×10−3×(T−298.15) + 2.303× RT/F × pH (5)

where T is the operation temperature (353.15 K), and the pH of 1 M KOH at 80 °C (353.15 K) is 12.5±0.1. E0Ag=AgCl = 0.1732 V (vs: SHE) is the standard potential versus standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) and is calculated according to Eq. (1).

The kinetic potential loss can be obtained using a Tafel (Eq. (6)) from the iR-corrected polarization curve at low current density region,

ΔEkinetic = b×log(j/j0) − Erev,OER (6)

where j0 is the exchange current density, j is the current density, and b is the Tafel slope and can be determined by fitting the low-current region (dominated by charge-transfer processes) of the polarization curve. The ohmic potential loss can be obtained using Ohm’s law (Eq. (7)),

ΔEohmic = HFR×j (7)

Thus, the mass transport potential loss can be obtained by Eq. (8):

ΔEmasstransport(j) = Eanode(j) − Erev,OER − ΔEkinetic(j) − ΔEohmic(j) (8)

Computational methods
All spin-polarized DFT calculations were conducted using the Vienna ab initio simulation package within the projected-augmented wave method58,59. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof functional was used to describe the exchange-correlation interaction60. The DFT+U method was utilized to correct the self-interaction error with Hubbard U parameters of 3.32, 5.30, and 6.20 eV for Co, Fe, and Ni, respectively61,62. The convergence criteria of the electronic total energy and structure relaxation were set to 10−5 eV and 0.05 eV Å-1, respectively. A plane wave energy cutoff of 450 eV was applied.

DFT method: The Brillouin zone was sampled using the Gamma scheme with a 1×2×1 k-point grid for the surface models with 5 atomic layers of LiCo2O4 63. A vacuum thickness of 16 Å was added along the z direction to avoid periodic interactions, and the dipole correction was applied as well. The (111) surface was selected for exploring the catalytic activity, as it is the most stable surface of the spinel structures64. The doped structure was generated by the special quasi-random structures algorithm implemented in the ATAT package65 and the most energetically favorable one was then selected for the activity and stability studies66. The OER activity was evaluated by the minimum overpotential required for the four elementary reactions given by:

*+H2O(l) → OH*+H++e− (9)

OH* → O*+H++e− (10)

O*+H2O(l) → OOH*+H++e− (11)

OOH* → O2+H++e− (12)

where * represents a surface site. The reaction free energy of these elementary steps was calculated as: ΔG=ΔE+ZPE−TΔS=ΔE+ΔGcorr, where ΔE is the adsorption energy, ZPE represents zero-point energy, and ΔS is the entropy change at 300 K. Free energy corrections were explicitly calculated per 67:

ΔGcorr = ZPE + ∫Cp dT−TS (13)

with vibrational frequencies computed for all intermediates at 300 K and 1 atm (Table S16). The catalyst stability was assessed by the Strongly Constrained and Appropriately Normed (SCAN) functional and calculated bulk Pourbaix diagram68,69. In SCAN calculations, the plane-wave energy cut-off was 520 eV. The electronic energy and structure relaxation were converged to 10−5 eV and 0.02 eV Å−1, respectively. The k-point grid density was 100 per reciprocal volume.

The Hubbard U parameters for Ni, Fe, and Co were empirically calibrated by fitting to experimental redox potentials of their corresponding metal oxides (Table S17)70. This approach ensures the computed U values accurately reproduce redox energetics critical to surface catalytic processes.

Surface model construction: To construct a reasonable surface model, three principles governed surface model construction: (1) We constructed the NiFePd-doped LCO bulk structure by optimizing 128 quasi-random structures and selecting the most stable one. It is observed that the Ni and Fe dopants tend to be located with each other, while the Pt and Ni dopants sit away from each other. These chemical insights were applied to construct the complex LCFNPdO catalyst surface; (2) Based on previous studies, the (111) facet is the most stable surface in spinel LCO and is therefore used as a surface model; (3) The presence of Pd in the sublayer is more stable than that on the top layer (Formation energy difference: −0.10 eV). Meanwhile, the more active Ni and Fe are often exposed on the topmost layer71,72. The final surface structure model was finally determined by considering all these factors.

All relevant adsorption sites on LCNFPdO were evaluated, including top sites of Co, Fe, and Ni atoms and Ni-Co bridge sites (Table S18). Structural relaxation revealed: (1) Intermediates at Ni/Co top sites consistently migrated to Ni-Co bridge sites, producing identical structures and energies; (2) Fe sites exhibited poor catalytic activity despite electronic modulation effects. The Ni-Co bridge site was consequently identified as the optimal active center.

Magnetic configuration: To address magnetic complexity in transition metal systems, we implemented a rigorous configuration selection protocol. The pristine slab model was first optimized to determine its lowest-energy magnetic moment configuration; Identical NUPDOWN values were subsequently applied to corresponding adsorbate systems; All configurations must satisfy four criteria: absence of antiferromagnetic ordering, adherence to the ΔGOOH−ΔGOH scaling relationship (2.8–3.3 V), total magnetization within 4 μB tolerance, and the selection of the lowest-energy state for multiple valid configurations; Systems failing these criteria were recalculated with NUPDOWN adjustments (±1 μB increments) and modified initial moments. Total magnetization data for all configurations are documented in Table S19.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript presents a multi-element doping strategy (Ni, Fe, Pd) to enhance the stability of LiCoO2 (LCO) for OER, mitigating surface reconstruction. While the experimental work is thorough and the reported improvements in OER performance are noteworthy, the manuscript lacks the mechanistic depth and conceptual clarity expected for publication in Nature Communications. The conclusions rely largely on macroscopic observations without sufficient atomic-level insight. A more rigorous theoretical framework is needed to support the proposed structure–function relationships. Key concerns are outlined below.
1. Ambiguity in doping mechanism: (1) The authors state that Ni and Pd doping increases the Co valence state while simultaneously suppressing its oxidation. These statements appear contradictory, as a higher Co valence is typically associated with increased oxidation behavior. This inconsistency should be addressed. Additionally, the explanation that the increase in Co valence arises solely from the introduction of low-valence Ni and Pd is overly simplistic. The Co valence state is influenced by several factors, such as the electronegativity of the dopants, orbital hybridization and the possible generation of oxygen vacancies due to valence mismatch. A more thorough investigation of these underlying mechanisms is necessary to support this conclusion, rather than relying on the dopants’ valence states alone.
(2) A clear mechanistic rationale of mitigating reconstruction should be provided. The authors report that LCNFPdO undergoes reconstruction into a spinel-type LiCo2O4 phase during OER, but do not clarify how multi-element doping alters the reconstruction pathway to favor this specific structure. If reconstruction is indeed observed, evidenced by the formation of LiCo2O4, then the claim of “mitigating reconstruction” is not accurate. It would be more appropriate to state that doping induces the formation of a stable spinel reconstruction layer. The authors are encouraged to elaborate on how this reconstructed structure contributes to enhanced stability. Additionally, it remains unclear what the final reconstruction product of undoped LCO is? Does it also form LiCo2O4?
(3) The individual roles of Ni, Fe, and Pd are not clearly distinguished. Possible synergistic or antagonistic effects between dopants are not discussed. A systematic investigation, such as single-element doping experiments or theoretical simulations, would clarify the contributions of each element.
2. Limited insight into mass transport mechanism: The authors claimed that the doping of Fe and Pd can enhance the electronic conductivity and gas transport properties, which fast reaction kinetics and rapid removal of bubbles. However, the conclusion is based solely on macroscopic observations (bubble statistics and limiting current density), the underlying mechanism remains speculative. Does Pd affect the wettability of the catalyst surface or reduce bubble adhesion? or could Fe doping alter local charge distributions to facilitate ion transport?
3. Inconsistencies in data interpretation: (1) The introduction notes that Fe is prone to dissolution under OER conditions (Line 69), yet Table S3 shows no Fe loss after extended high-temperature and high-current operation for LCNFPdO catalyst. This discrepancy should be clarified.
(2) An activation process is reported during the initial CV cycles (line 111), indicated by increased current density. However, no explanation is offered. Could this be due to the formation of a reconstructed layer, and if so, how does that align with the claim of suppressed reconstruction?
(3) The discussion (line 249) uses O-K edge sXAS and O 1s XPS to support more adsorbed oxygen species on LCNFPdO, due to reconstructed surface. Yet previous findings indicate that LCO undergoes more extensive surface reconstruction. Why is OH adsorption not more prominent in LCO? This inconsistency requires further clarification.
4. Insufficient experimental details: (1) The method for post-reaction sample collection for XRD and XAS is not described. Please include details such as how powders were collected and prepared.
(2) Key parameters for AEMWE testing are missing, including membrane electrode assembly method, catalyst loading, and membrane type.
5. Inappropriate language and formatting errors: (1) Avoid superlative terms like “the longest reported lifetime” or “none of these strategies”, unless supported by comprehensive comparative data.
(3) Figure 3e is discussed twice with nearly identical description (Lines 161 and 245).
(4) Line 191 links the peak intensity of the 104-diffraction pattern to structural disorder. This requires a citation or clearer justification.
(5) Line 252 contains a double comma and should be corrected; Line 333 incorrectly places a period before the citation " (Figure 39)".

### Reviewer 3

The authors have screened a series of element-doped LiCoO₂ materials and identified LiCo₀.₇₉Ni₀.₁Fe₀.₁Pd₀.₀₁O₂ (LCNFPdO) as the most active catalyst for alkaline water electrolysis. While the ex-situ characterization of LCNFPdO is comprehensive, the manuscript lacks a robust discussion—and corresponding experimental evidence—linking the reconstructed surface structure to the observed OER performance. Furthermore, the reported cell voltage of 1.58 V at 2.5 A cm⁻² (iR-corrected; ~2.1 V without compensation) appears impressive, but a fair comparison to state-of-the-art catalysts should be made using uncorrected voltages. My detailed comments follow:
1. The authors acknowledge Li leaching during OER, yet no direct structural comparison is made between LCO and LCNFPdO after reconstruction. In Fig. 1b, the CV curves for LCO and LCNFPdO cross in opposite ways before and after cycling—suggesting fundamentally different surface evolution. The manuscript should include a more in-depth characterization/discussion on the structure and the structural difference after reconstruction and how these differences relate to the observed OER activity. Moreover, what chemical understanding was obtained after screening/characterizing/testing a series of dopants was not discussed.
2. In Figs. S21–S22, the authors claim that LCNFPdO is less oxidized post-OER than LCO. However, the Co L₃-edge sXAS peak shifts in Fig. S21 are subtle and not convincingly resolved. Likewise, the Co 2p XPS fits in Fig. S22 appear overly broad for the Co²⁺ and Co⁴⁺ components—e.g., the Co²⁺ peak for LCO in Fig. S22c seems significantly wider than that for LCNFPdO. I recommend re-fitting/re-analyzing these results after carefully reviewing the peaking fitting constraints.
3. Almost all characterizations and oxygen adsorption were collected ex-situ. Given that bias removal and air exposure can alter the surface, the authors should either perform in-situ or—at minimum—provide evidence demonstrating that these ex-situ spectra reliably reflect the status of surface under OER conditions.
4. The manuscript attributes higher currents in LCNFPdO partly to enhanced mass transport. However, LSV data were recorded in the mixed-kinetic/diffusion regime, so mass-transport effects are conflated with intrinsic kinetics. A deconvolution of kinetic and diffusion contributions should be made to support the claim. Additionally, hydrophobicity differences at the level reported are too small and not statistically meaningful to draw firm conclusions (contact angles 30.1° vs. 32.3°).
5. Reporting 1.58 V at 2.5 A cm⁻² only after iR correction may mislead readers regarding practical performance. The authors should also compare the uncorrected performance for LCNFPdO with the state-of-the-art catalysts (Table S10). The author may refer to this comprehensive performance summary: Supplementary Table 2 in Nature Catalysis 7, 944–952 (2024). This will allow a fair, “apples-to-apples” comparison under realistic operating conditions.

### Reviewer 4

In the manuscript by Wang et al., titled "Sustainable Water Oxidation Enabled by a Complex-doped Cobalt Oxide Electrode", the authors present a very interesting combined experimental and theoretical investigation of a LiCoO2-based electrocatalyst doped with Ni, Fe, and Pd for the oxygen evolution reaction. The proposed system exhibits high catalytic activity, delivering 2.5 A cm-2 at 1.58 V, while maintaining excellent long-term stability. The authors demonstrate that complex doping suppresses cobalt redox during OER, effectively mitigating surface reconstruction, enhancing electrochemical stability, improving surface conductivity, and facilitating gas removal—thereby boosting mechanical robustness. I find these findings highly significant, as they directly address the persistent challenge of catalyst degradation under industrial OER conditions, and in my view, merit publication in Nature Communications. The work is well-written and scientifically sound. However, several critical points should be addressed to enhance the overall quality of the manuscript before it can be recommended for publication.
1. The authors constructed the NiFePd-doped LiCoO2 bulk structure by optimizing 128 quasi-random configurations and selecting the most stable one. However, it’s not clear how the surface shown in Fig. S39 was built. Different surface cuts can expose different dopants and lead to variations in stability, so some clarification is needed.
2. OER intermediates (*OH, *O, *OOH) were optimized on both LiCoO2 and NiFePd-doped LiCoO2 surfaces. However, the doped surface contains a large number of non-equivalent adsorption sites with potentially different activities. It’s not clear how the optimization was performed in this case—were all relevant sites considered, or just one specific configuration? Some clarification is needed. Moreover, the POSCAR files of the optimized key structures should be provided in the Supplementary Information to ensure reproducibility of the results.
3. The manuscript assumes a conventional single-site OER mechanism as shown in Supplementary Note 2. However, given the doped and reconstructed nature of the surface, with multiple metal centers in close proximity, could dual-site or cooperative mechanisms play a role? It would be useful if the authors could comment on whether such possibilities were considered and how the dual-site mechanism can affect the theoretical overpotential.
4. The choice of Hubbard U parameters for Ni, Fe, and Co should be justified. Have the authors performed any self-consistent calculations to determine the U values? The U = 6.2 eV used for Ni appears somewhat large in my opinion.
5. It is really disappointing how the authors calculated the changes in free energy, especially ΔG_corr. They simply used approximate values for zero-point energy and entropy corrections suggested in early works by Nørskov for metal surfaces. This methodology is outdated, especially for a study submitted to a high-impact journal like Nature Communications. Such corrections can vary significantly for complex metal oxides and should be explicitly calculated for each intermediate. Moreover, the manuscript does not explain how solvent effects were treated, which is critical, as solvation can substantially impact the computed free energy values.
6. The system contains transition metal atoms with unpaired d-electrons (Fe, Co, and Ni), and in my experience, it can be very challenging to identify the correct spin ordering in such complex systems. The authors should clearly state the magnetic configuration used and explain how it was chosen to ensure the lowest-energy structure.
Overall, this work addresses an important topic and may be suitable for Nature Communications, but in its current form, it requires substantial revision before it can be considered for publication.

First, we would like to highlight that Fig. 1a offers an experimental basis for understanding

temperatures. Generally, Single-element-doped samples (e.g., LCFO, LCNO, LCPdO)

To further get the thermodynamic insights, we added more DFT calculations. As shown in
Figure R4, all samples except for LCNPdO are on the right side of the volcano plot,

the above experimental results, the ternary-element-doped LCO is exclusively superior to

Fe, and Pd are co-doped simultaneously, Pd further optimizes the electronic structure of
LCO compared with the NiFe-doped one, resulting in the lowest theoretical overpotential.

Fe and Pd to optimize the electronic configuration of LCO and achieve the best OER
activity. It should be noted that Pd doping is also favorable to improve the stability of LCO

The urgent need to address instability in cobalt-based oxide electrodes represents a

1. Please provide a clear and quantitative definition of “reconstruction extent” and specify

Response:
Thank you for acknowledging our work and proposing those insightful comments. We
proposed the concept of “reconstruction extent” in our previously published paper (Chem,
9, 7: 1645-1657, 2023)12. Here, we defined the reconstruction extent as the degree of the
reconstruction level, and we can evaluate it by comparing the thickness of the
reconstructed layer during the OER. Since the formation of this reconstructed layer

“The MEAs were fabricated using a hand spray-coating method for both the anode and
cathode catalyst layers. The anode catalyst ink was prepared by dispersing the catalyst
powder in a mixed solvent of deionized water and isopropanol (mass ratio = 1:4:5).
Subsequently, 5 wt% Nafion solution was added, resulting in a Nafion content of 7 wt% in
the final ink. The ink was ultrasonicated for 1 hour to ensure homogeneous dispersion and
then uniformly sprayed onto a nickel foam substrate (Kunshan Shengshijingxin New
Material Co., Ltd, China). The anode catalyst loading was controlled at 10.0 ± 0.5 mg cm-2,
determined by weight difference before and after coating. For the cathode, a 5 wt% Pt/C
catalyst (Alfa Aesar) was used. The ink formulation consisted of catalyst, deionized water,
and isopropanol in a weight ratio of 1:8:9. After adding 5 wt% Nafion solution (final Nafion
content 10 wt%), the ink was ultrasonicated for 1 hour and then sprayed onto a carbon
paper substrate (TGP-H-120T, Toray). The Pt loading was 0.5 mg cm-2.
A commercial Sustainion® membrane (X37-50, Grade T, Dioxide Materials) was employed
as the anion exchange membrane for all single-cell tests. Prior to use, the membrane was
pre-treated by soaking in 1 M KOH for 12 hours to ensure full ion exchange. The MEA was
assembled with an active geometric area of 1.0 cm2 (as shown in Fig. 6a). The single cell
hardware was composed of nickel-coated stainless-steel endplates to ensure chemical
stability in alkaline media.
All electrochemical measurements were conducted in 1 M KOH electrolyte, supplied to
both anode and cathode chambers. Polarization curves were recorded at 80 °C by a Gamry
5000E electrochemical workstation with a scan rate of 5 mV s-1. The durability of the MEA
was evaluated by operating the cell at a constant current density of 500 mA cm-2 at 60 °C.
High-frequency resistance (HFR) was measured via EIS using a Gamry 5000E
electrochemical workstation over a frequency range from 1 MHz to 1 Hz at a cell potential
of 1.8 V. The HFR was obtained from the intercept of the Nyquist plot with the real axis.”
These revisions ensure that all key parameters and procedures related to AEMWE testing
are presented with sufficient clarity and reproducibility.

EQCM measurements conducted during OER operation, which monitor lithium
deintercalation in real time (Fig. 3f-g) since there is no obvious leaching of other metals
from ICP-MS. As redox-active materials, cobalt valence in LCO is dependent on Li
composition. By monitoring the mass change caused by Li loss, we could predict the trend
of cobalt valence change. These results agree with our postmortem characterizations,
demonstrating consistent Co oxidation and surface transformation metrics.
Moreover, in this revision, we include in-situ Raman spectroscopy data that clearly show
the emergence of two characteristic peaks at ~ 465 cm-1 (E mode) and ~565 cm-1 (A
g 1g

under the same applied potential, confirming that its reconstruction is more limited and
corroborating STEM (Fig. S15-18), XAFS (Fig. 3a-b), and TOF-SIMS (Fig. 3e) findings in
our manuscript.
Finally, the above findings are consistent with our previous operando investigations
published in Nature Catalysis, 4, 212–222, 2021. With operando XAFS, it was found that
the higher cobalt valence in LCO made it more resistant to further oxidation during OER—
an observation that aligns well with our EQCM results and confirms the consistency of our
ex-situ analyses.

supporting operando XAFS data all converge to affirm that the ex-situ spectroscopy
measurements used in our study provide a reliable depiction of the catalytic surface under

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In the manuscript by Wang et al., titled "Sustainable Water Oxidation Enabled by a
Complex-doped Cobalt Oxide Electrode", the authors present a very interesting
combined experimental and theoretical investigation of a LiCoO2-based electrocatalyst
doped with Ni, Fe, and Pd for the oxygen evolution reaction. The proposed system
exhibits high catalytic activity, delivering 2.5 A cm-2 at 1.58 V, while maintaining excellent
long-term stability. The authors demonstrate that complex doping suppresses cobalt
redox during OER, effectively mitigating surface reconstruction, enhancing
electrochemical stability, improving surface conductivity, and facilitating gas removal—
thereby boosting mechanical robustness. I find these findings highly significant, as they
directly address the persistent challenge of catalyst degradation under industrial OER
conditions, and in my view, merit publication in Nature Communications. The work is
well-written and scientifically sound. However, several critical points should be
addressed to enhance the overall quality of the manuscript before it can be
recommended for publication.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive evaluation of our work and for
recognizing the significance of our findings. At the same time, we highly appreciate the
reviewer’s critical comments, which are constructive and valuable for improving the clarity
and overall quality of the manuscript. We have carefully revised the manuscript accordingly,
and our detailed responses to each point are provided below.
Comment 1. The authors constructed the NiFePd-doped LiCoO bulk structure by
2
optimizing 128 quasi-random configurations and selecting the most stable one.
However, it’s not clear how the surface shown in Fig. S39 was built. Different surface
cuts can expose different dopants and lead to variations in stability, so some clarification
is needed.
Response: Thank you for your comments. The NiFePd-doped LCO bulk structure was
determined by optimizing 128 quasi-random structures and selecting the most stable one.
Our calculations reveal that Ni and Fe dopants exhibit clustering tendencies, while Pd
and Ni dopants preferentially occupy separated sites. To determine the energetically
favorable surface structure for the complex LCFNPdO catalyst, we applied these chemical
insights to surface structure ordering. Next, consistent with established literature45, we
adopted the (111) facet of spinel LCO as our surface model due to its superior stability.
Finally, we explored the energetics of the different terminations. We found Pd prefers
sublayer positions over top-layer exposure (formation energy difference: -0.10 eV).
Meanwhile, Ni and Fe elements are often exposed on the topmost layers in the studied
models46,47. These considerations collectively identify the finalized structure model. We
have added the above details in Supplementary Note 2 of the revised SI, which is also
copied below for your reference:
“To construct a reasonable surface model, three principles governed surface model
construction: (1) We constructed the NiFePd-doped LCO bulk structure by optimizing 128
quasi-random structures and selecting the most stable one. It is observed that the Ni and
Fe dopants tend to be located with each other, while the Pt and Ni dopants sit away from
each other. These chemical insights were applied to construct the complex LCFNPdO
catalyst surface; (2) Based on previous studies, the (111) facet is the most stable surface
in spinel LCO and is therefore used as a surface model; (3) The presence of Pd in the
sublayer is more stable than that on the top layer (Formation energy difference: -0.10 eV).
Meanwhile, the more active Ni and Fe are often exposed on the topmost layer. The final
surface structure model was finally determined by considering all these factors.”
Comment 2. OER intermediates (*OH, *O, *OOH) were optimized on both LiCoO2 and
NiFePd-doped LiCoO2 surfaces. However, the doped surface contains a large number
of non-equivalent adsorption sites with potentially different activities. It’s not clear how
the optimization was performed in this case—were all relevant sites considered, or just
one specific configuration? Some clarification is needed. Moreover, the POSCAR files
of the optimized key structures should be provided in the Supplementary Information to
ensure reproducibility of the results.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. We have systematically evaluated all relevant
adsorption sites on the NiFePd-doped LCO surface, including top sites of Co, Fe, and Ni
atoms and bridge sites between Ni and Co (as referenced in Table R7). During structural
relaxation, intermediates initially placed at top sites of Ni or Co consistently migrated to
bridge sites between Ni and Co, resulting in identical final configurations and Gibbs free
energies. For Fe sites, they play a more important role in optimizing the electronic structure
of surrounding atoms, and their poor activity is insufficient to serve as active sites. Finally,
we chose the bridge site as the most reasonable active site. The key structures are
provided in Supplementary Note 2 of the revised SI, and we have added the clarification
as follows:
“All relevant adsorption sites on NiFePd-doped LCO were evaluated, including top sites
of Co, Fe, and Ni atoms and Ni-Co bridge sites (Table S18). Structural relaxation revealed:
(1) Intermediates at Ni/Co top sites consistently migrated to Ni-Co bridge sites, producing
identical structures and energies; (2) Fe sites exhibited poor catalytic activity despite
electronic modulation effects. The Ni-Co bridge site was consequently identified as the
optimal active center.”

Comment 3. The manuscript assumes a conventional single-site OER mechanism as
shown in Supplementary Note 2. However, given the doped and reconstructed nature of
the surface, with multiple metal centers in close proximity, could dual-site or cooperative
mechanisms play a role? It would be useful if the authors could comment on whether
such possibilities were considered and how the dual-site mechanism can affect the
theoretical overpotential.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful suggestion. It is widely acknowledged
that the surface state under electrochemical working conditions plays a key role in
determining the reaction mechanisms. Before diving into the dual-site mechanism, we
first examined the catalyst surface state under typical OER working conditions in alkaline
environments through the surface Pourbaix diagram analysis (Figure R15). The dashed
line represents the OER onset potential, which falls within the clean surface regime (our
slab model). Meanwhile, the potential from O* bridge adsorption (O* model) to O* bridge
an O* (Fe) adsorption is 1.83 V vs. RHE, which is higher than the typical OER reaction
potential. Therefore, the selection of surface adsorption species in our model is
reasonable. Specifically, at potentials below 0.60 V vs. SHE, the surface remains clean.
As the potential increases to 0.60-1.00 V vs. SHE, oxygen adsorption occurs exclusively
at bridge sites (O* model). For further adsorption, Co, Ni, and Fe top sites are potential
candidates. However, additional oxygen adsorption at Co and Ni top sites directly
generates O due to coordination saturation. For Fe sites, the potential required for
2
further oxygen adsorption at pH=14 reaches 1.00 V vs. SHE, indicating an energetically
unfavorable process. Consequently, the saturated coordination environment around
active sites makes dual-site catalysis unlikely.

Comment 6. The system contains transition metal atoms with unpaired d-electrons (Fe,
Co, and Ni), and in my experience, it can be very challenging to identify the correct spin
ordering in such complex systems. The authors should clearly state the magnetic
configuration used and explain how it was chosen to ensure the lowest-energy structure.
Response: We completely agree with the reviewer that our studied systems are complex.
In this work, we applied the ferromagnetic state for adsorption energies calculations due
to the prohibitive computational costs in exploring the large antiferromagnetic states.
To keep calculations consistent, we implemented the following procedure: First, we
deliberately optimized the surface structure to determine the lowest-energy magnetic
configuration. We then constrained the total magnetic moment of the corresponding
adsorption systems to this determined value. All calculations were required to satisfy four
criteria: (1) no antiferromagnetic ordering appears; (2) the calculated ∆G - ∆G
OOH OH
adheres to the scaling relationship (approximately 2.8–3.3); (3) the total magnetization
of the entire model remains within a range of about 4 μB; and (4) When multiple magnetic
configurations satisfy conditions (1)-(3), we select the configuration with the lowest
energy. When calculations failed to meet these criteria, we recalculated with adjusted
NUPDOWN values (±1 μB increments) and modified initial moments. The total
magnetization values for all systems are listed in Table R10. We have supplemented the
relevant statements in the Method section:
“To address magnetic complexity in transition metal systems, we implemented a rigorous
configuration selection protocol: The pristine slab model was first optimized to determine
its lowest-energy magnetic moment configuration; Identical NUPDOWN values were
subsequently applied to corresponding adsorbate systems; All configurations must
satisfy four criteria: absence of antiferromagnetic ordering, adherence to the ∆G -
OOH
∆G scaling relationship (2.8-3.3 V, considering the influence of solvents), total
OH

multiple valid configurations; Systems failing these criteria were recalculated with

## Paper

## Abstract

Achieving sustainable water oxidation presents significant challenges, particularly employing cobalt-based electrocatalysts. Despite promising activities, many cobalt-based electrocatalysts undergo in-situ partial restructuring into disordered (oxy)hydroxides, as indicated by the Pourbaix diagram. This restructuring typically degrades structural integrity and electronic conductivity, undermining catalytic stability. Here, we propose a complex doping strategy to stabilize LiCoO2, a cobalt oxide that can be sourced from spent lithium-ion batteries, for sustainable water oxidation. Specifically, by co-doping LiCoO2 with Ni, Fe, and Pd, we mitigate the reconstructed extent of the in-situ generated spinel phase during water oxidation reaction and enhance electrochemical stability. Furthermore, complex doping improves the surface conductivity and facilitates gas removal, boosting mechanical robustness. Consequently, the optimized LiCo0.79Ni0.1Fe0.1Pd0.01O2 achieves a competitive water oxidation stability of over 2000 hours. Additionally, in membrane electrolyzer tests, LiCo0.79Ni0.1Fe0.1Pd0.01O2 outperforms the benchmark RuO2, delivering 2.5 A cm−2 at 1.58 V and maintaining stability for over 1400 hours. By elucidating the role of each dopant in LiCo0.79Ni0.1Fe0.1Pd0.01O2, this work offers critical insights for the rational design of sustainable water splitting electrodes.

---

## Introduction

Coupling water electrolysis technologies with renewable electricity to produce green hydrogen represents a promising approach for mitigating the intermittency issue of renewable energies and reducing CO2 emissions1. The performance of catalysts in a water electrolyzer significantly impacts the electricity consumption (approximately 70%–90% of the total hydrogen production cost) and operation durability (typically 10,000–100,000 h)2,3. Substantial research has been dedicated to developing low-cost electrocatalysts for water electrolysis, focusing on the anodic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) that poses a significant energy barrier4,5. Despite the considerable achievements in understanding the water-splitting process and developing electrocatalysts, significant challenges remain in transferring the high performance demonstrated by many designed electrocatalysts in rotating disk electrode (RDE) setups to practical electrolyzer applications. For instance, NiFeOxHy, widely accepted as one of the most active OER electrocatalysts in a typical RDE setup, demonstrated considerably poor activity in the membrane electrode assembly (MEA) configuration6–8. Moreover, they can leach Fe in “Fe-free” electrolytes, losing activity and posing threats to ion exchange membranes9. Beyond activity, stability is another big concern. Many OER electrocatalysts undergo alterations in their physicochemical properties due to in-situ reconstruction, a dynamic process that affects structural and catalytic stability10. For instance, cobalt oxides (e.g., Ba0.5Sr0.5Co0.8Fe0.2O3-delta, Co3O4) usually undergo partial reconstructions into layered (oxy)hydroxides, resulting in sacrificed crystallinity and loss of compositing elements11,12. Although this reconstruction can initially enhance activity, it may ultimately impair practical activity and long-term stability due to the less conductive nature of the reconstructed surface13–16. However, previous studies on catalyst reconstructions were usually conducted at ambient temperature and under small current densities17, which limits the applicability of their findings to practical electrolyzer conditions.

Layered LiCoO2 (LCO) is of particular interest among the various cobalt oxides due to the facile tunability of its cobalt redox and associated lithium composition18,19. Also, the abundant availability of LCO from spent lithium-ion batteries makes it an appealing material for recycling and repurposing in other energy applications20. Nevertheless, the intrinsic OER activity of LCO is limited due to the substantial potential barrier that must be overcome to trigger its favorable surface reconstructions18. Several strategies have been employed to enhance its activity, including elemental doping18,21, exfoliation22, cation insertion23, and electrochemical tuning19. While these strategies have shown various improvements, achieving an OER electrode that combines both high performance and long-term durability suitable for practical electrolyzer conditions remains a significant challenge.

Here, we report a complex doping method to improve the practical OER performance of LCO and clarify the critical role of each doping element. By manipulating the catalyst reconstruction extent under elevated electrolysis temperatures, we have developed a high-performance LiCo0.79Ni0.1Fe0.1Pd0.01O2 (LCNFPdO) electrocatalyst with good stability (over 2000 h) and activity that is competitive with benchmark catalysts.

Theoreticalcalculations
To understand the modulated performance, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations to investigate the OER stability and activity. Based on the preceding TEM analysis, the surface of LCO and LCNFPdO reconstructed into a LiCo2O4-type spinel structure. Moreover, the surface Li loss was close to 50% (Fig. 3f), and the ICP-MS data (Table S4) confirmed negligible dissolution of Co, Ni, Fe, or Pd for LCNFPdO after OER. As a result, a calculation model of Li0.5Co0.79Ni0.1Fe0.1Pd0.01O2 (i.e., Li0.5Co0.79Ni0.1Fe0.1Pd0.01O2) (Fig. 5a) was applied, which was identified as the most energetically stable configuration using the special quasi-random structures algorithm. The half-delithiated spinel phase model was consistent with previous reports18,35,36. We observed that the Ni and Fe dopants tended to be located with each other, while the Pd and Ni dopants remained separated. These chemical arrangement patterns were then used to construct the complex Li0.5Co0.79Ni0.1Fe0.1Pd0.01O2 catalyst surface for subsequent performance investigations (Fig. S42).

Figure 5b shows the calculated dissolution free energies (ΔGdiss) of LiCo2O4 and Li0.5Co0.79Ni0.1Fe0.1Pd0.01O2 (Supplementary data 1) at varying potentials in alkaline media. A higher ΔG value indicates greater catalyst instability under electrochemical working conditions. For LiCo2O4, as the applied potential shifts from 1.23 V to 2.00 V, the calculated ΔG decreases from 0.45 to 0.19 eV/atom. These large ΔG values suggest that LiCo2O4 is unstable under working conditions and tends to decompose into CoOOH(s) and LiOH(aq). This result is in line with our experimental observations. In contrast, doping with Ni, Fe, and Pd considerably reduces the ΔG to 0.21 eV/atom at 1.23 V and 0 eV/atom at 2.00 V. Notably, when the applied potential exceeds 1.55 V, the ΔG becomes 0.03 eV/atom. This value falls well within the stable region where kinetics, driven by solid-solid phase transformation49, play a key role. Specifically, the formation Co3O4(s) and NiPdO3(s) remarkably lowers the ΔG, consequently enhancing the catalyst stability of LCNFPdO under operating conditions. This result aligns well with our experimental observations, as no obvious leaching was detected for LCNFPdO via ICP-MS (Table S4), unlike the Fe-containing hydroxides9. Close examination of the decomposition products reveal that this enhanced catalyst stability primarily arises from the Pd dopant, which facilitates the formation of NiPdO3(s) and Li0.5Co0.79Ni0.1Fe0.1Pd0.01O2(s).

Determining the surface adsorption state under electrochemical working conditions is a crucial first step in studying surface activity. Therefore, we calculated the surface Pourbaix diagram for LCNFPdO, as shown in Fig. 5c. Under typical alkaline OER conditions (e.g., pH = 14, potential = 1.6 V), the catalyst surface is covered by O* at the Ni-Co bridge site. At potentials higher than 1.8 V, O* adsorption becomes accessible at the Co, Ni, and Fe top sites. Coupling two adsorbed O* species at these top sites directly forms O2 gas during DFT structure optimization, a result attributed to the weak binding of O* on the transition metal oxide50. This potential-independent O2 formation indicates that an oxide pathway mechanism is unlikely for LCNFPdO. Furthermore, a surface with oxygen vacancies is only stable at potentials below −0.61 V vs. SHE, which also rules out the lattice oxygen mechanism for OER. In light of these findings, the adsorbate evolution reaction mechanism was applied to investigate the OER activity in this work.

To elucidate the role of each dopant, we calculated the OER activity for LCNFPdO and six other systems for comparison (Table S14 and Supplementary data 1). With the exception of the LCNPdO system, all catalysts reside on the right side of the volcano, as shown in Fig. 5d. This indicates that the formation of O* is the potential-determining step (PDS) due to weak O* binding. For single-element doping, the calculated overpotentials (ηOER) for LCFO (0.90 V) and LCPdO (0.76 V) are higher than that of pristine LCO (0.68 V), suggesting poorer OER activity. In contrast, Ni doping reduces the overpotential to 0.61 V, indicating enhanced activity. Among the binary-doped systems, LCFPdO shows a slight improvement over LCO with a calculated η of 0.67 V. The LCNFO system exhibits significantly enhanced activity with an overpotential of 0.54 V, which can be attributed to electronic optimization between Ni and Fe. In contrast, the LCNPdO system has a higher overpotential of 0.77 V and notably undergoes a PDS shift from O* to OOH* formation, highlighting Pd’s role in electronic restructuring. For the ternary-doped system, LCNFPdO achieves the lowest overpotential of 0.46 V, suggesting that Pd further optimizes the NiFe electronic framework. Taken together, these results indicate that Ni is a pivotal active site that synergizes with Co, and its activity is further amplified by Fe through electronic cooperation. To establish fundamental mechanistic insights, we conducted integrated Bader charge and density of states (DOS) analyses. Bader charge analysis (Table S9) reveals that Ni/Fe co-doping facilitates a substantial charge transfer enhancement of about 0.3e on Co sites. Concurrently, a 0.1e enhancement in charge transfer at Co sites was observed for LCPdO relative to LCO. This demonstrates Pd’s significant contribution to electronic structure modulation. Complementarily, total DOS analysis (Fig. S43 and Supplementary data 1) demonstrates Fe-doping reduces the band gap by 0.4 eV, while LCNFPdO manifests metallic conductivity through further electronic restructuring. The enhanced conductivity is an important indicator of catalysts. Collectively, these synergistic electronic modifications constitute the fundamental mechanism driving enhanced catalytic activity.

Based on our experimental results, we speculate that the mass transport of reactants (H2O) and products (O2) may also influence OER performance. Therefore, the adsorption energies for H2O and O2 were calculated as shown in Fig. 5e. The calculated O2 adsorption energies for LCNFPdO and LCO were 1.10 eV and 0.35 eV, respectively. This result suggests that LCNFPdO possesses weakened O2 adsorption compared to LCO. Such weakened O2 adsorption facilitates the desorption of O2 from the electrode surface. The calculated H2O adsorption energies for LCNFPdO and LCO were −1.07 eV and −0.33 eV, respectively. This result suggests that LCNFPdO has a stronger tendency for H2O adsorption compared with LCO, which is beneficial for enhancing OER efficiency. Comprehensive comparison in Fig. S44 demonstrates Fe doping inhibits H2O/O2 adsorption, whereas Ni and Pd synergistically enhances surface binding. This adsorption dichotomy stems from Co-site electronic modulation: augmented charge transfer elevates valence states and local electronegativity, intensifying adsorbate interactions.

AEMWE performance
To verify the practical application, the catalysts studied were fabricated into the MEA for the AEMWE tests (Fig. 6a). At the same voltage, LCNFPdO achieved a current density much larger than those of RuO2, IrO2, α-Co(OH)2, Co3O4, and β-Co(OH)2 (Fig. 6b). This performance was also accompanied by a lower polarization impedance (Fig. 6c). With iR correction, LCNFPdO delivered 2.5 A cm−2 at only 1.58 V (Fig. 6b), suggesting great application potential. The three-electrode electrolyzer tests confirmed a lower mass transport resistance of LCNFPdO than LCO, as shown in Fig. S45. In addition, the AEMWE cell with LCNFPdO as the anode sustained the current density of 500 mA cm−2 without any degradation for over 1420 h (Fig. 6d). Such a performance is comparable to the highest values reported for cobalt-oxide–based electrocatalysts (Table S15).

Discussion
This work proposed a complex-element doping strategy to yield a sustainable cobalt oxide electrode for highly active and stable OER. The multi-element doping mitigated the reconstructed extent of the in-situ formed spinel surface during the OER, forming a stable surface with significantly enhanced activity at industrial temperatures. The obtained LCNFPdO outperformed RuO2 in OER activity and demonstrated stability of over 2000 h without serious degradation, setting a benchmark for cobalt-based OER electrocatalysts. In addition, the mechanism underlying the complex doping-improved performance was also clarified: (a) The introduction of lower-valence Ni and Pd dopants increased the cobalt valence in pristine LCNFPdO, mitigated its in-situ cobalt oxidation during the OER, thus reducing surface reconstruction extent and improving OER stability. Furthermore, the reconstructed LiCo2O4-type spinel phase of low thickness favored a higher intrinsic OER activity by facilitating the adsorption of oxygen intermediates on the catalyst surface, contributing to higher OER activity. (c) The doping of Fe and Pd also enhanced the electronic conductivity and gas transport properties, resulting in fast reaction kinetics and rapid removal of bubbles. Shortly, these results shed light on the directional designing of active OER catalysts by multiple elements doping and represent a significant advancement in manipulating in situ generated active species to prepare high-performance OER catalysts at industrial temperatures.
